title: 1.5.12 Decompose Getting to School
description: Six tasks, your own categories, and one thing the grouping tells you that the list did not. AI-graded with hints.

aiGrader.rubricTitle: Decompose Getting to School — AI-graded rubric
aiGrader.prompt:
Everything you need is in 1.5.8 (Decomposition) and the worked example in 1.5.11 — go back and reread them if you get stuck. Your own everyday words are fine.

The problem is: get to school on time tomorrow.

1. Decompose it into at least six smaller tasks. List them. (1.5.8)

2. Group those tasks into two or three categories of your own choosing. Name each category. (1.5.11)

3. Now look at your groups. Name one thing the grouping showed you that the flat list did not — a task you had forgotten, a category that turned out much fuller than the others, or a task that belonged somewhere surprising.

4. Pick one of your tasks and say whether it is still too big. Could it be decomposed further? If yes, break it down. If no, say why it is already small enough. (1.5.8)

rubric.title: At least six tasks, and they are genuinely separate
rubric.description: Student lists six or more distinct tasks that together make up getting to school. Deny if fewer than six, or if items are restatements of each other ('leave the house' and 'go outside').

rubric.title: Tasks are grouped into two or three named categories
rubric.description: Student sorts the tasks into two or three groups and gives each group a name. Any sensible grouping counts - by time (night before / morning / journey), by place, by who does it. Deny if the tasks are simply relisted, or if the groups have no names.

rubric.title: Q3: names something the grouping revealed
rubric.description: Student identifies a specific discovery from grouping - a forgotten task, an unexpectedly full category, or a task that belonged somewhere surprising. The most common real answer is that a large share of tasks belong to the night before. Deny if the answer only restates the categories or says grouping made it 'more organised' with no specific finding.

rubric.title: Q4: judges one task's size, with reasoning
rubric.description: Student picks one task and either breaks it down further into sub-steps, or argues it is already small enough. Credit either answer if the reasoning refers to whether the task is self-contained or whether someone could carry it out without asking a question. Deny if no judgement is given, or the judgement has no reason attached.
